# The equation we want to read {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

This note assumes familiar likelihood and ordinary Bayes' rule, but no measure
theory. Read these notes first, in order:

1. [Sets, functions, inverse images, and pushforwards](../Measure_Theory/sets-functions-and-pushforwards.qmd)
2. [Measure and probability foundations](../Measure_Theory/measure-probability-foundations.qmd)
3. [Lebesgue measure, integration, and densities](../Measure_Theory/lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd)

In particular, the third note explains null sets, absolute continuity,
dominating measures, and Radon-Nikodym derivatives with discrete, continuous,
and mixed examples.

Walker writes a posterior on a space of density functions in the form

$$
\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n})
=
\frac{\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n f(X_i)\right\}\Pi(df)}
{\int_{\mathcal D}\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n g(X_i)\right\}\Pi(dg)}.
\tag{1}
$$

The $d$ in $\Pi(df)$ is not “differentiate $\Pi$ with respect to $f$.”
Equation (1) is compact notation for a relationship between probability
measures. The fully explicit version appears below.

# Four appearances of d that should not be conflated

## 1. An ordinary calculus derivative

If $r(x)=x^2$, then

$$
\frac{dr}{dx}(x)=2x.
$$

This derivative describes the local rate of change of one function relative to
its input.

## 2. The dx in a Riemann integral

In elementary calculus,

$$
\int_a^b h(x)\,dx
$$

is introduced as the limit of sums $\sum_j h(x_j)\Delta x_j$. The $dx$
reminds us that interval widths are being used.

## 3. Integration with respect to a measure

Measure theory writes

$$
\int h(x)\,\mu(dx)
\quad\text{or}\quad
\int h\,d\mu.
$$

These mean “integrate $h$ with respect to the measure $\mu$.” The expression
$\mu(dx)$ is a notational marker for the integrator. It is not, by itself, the
measure of a literal infinitesimal interval around $x$.

Lebesgue integration makes the elementary notation precise:

$$
\int h(x)\,dx
=\int h(x)\,\lambda(dx),
$$

where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure.

## 4. A derivative of one measure with respect to another

If $P$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\nu$, written $P\ll\nu$, the
Radon-Nikodym theorem gives a measurable function

$$
p(x)=\frac{dP}{d\nu}(x)
$$

such that

$$
P(A)=\int_A p(x)\,\nu(dx)
\quad\text{for every measurable }A.
\tag{2}
$$

Here $dP/d\nu$ really is a derivative at the level of measures. A statistical
density is a Radon-Nikodym derivative.

The condition $P\ll\nu$ means

$$
\nu(A)=0\implies P(A)=0.
$$

Thus $P$ does not put positive mass where the reference measure $\nu$ sees a
null set. The theorem says that, under standard conditions, this is precisely
what allows $P$ to be represented by a weighting function relative to $\nu$.
No proof of the theorem is needed to interpret Walker's notation.

# How P(dx) covers discrete and continuous distributions

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$.

## Discrete case

If $P$ puts mass $p_j$ at $x_j$, then

$$
P=\sum_j p_j\delta_{x_j}
$$

and

$$
\int h(x)P(dx)=\sum_j p_jh(x_j).
$$

In this case $P(\{x_j\})=p_j$.

## Continuous case

If $P$ has density $p=dP/d\lambda$ relative to Lebesgue measure, then the
precise measure identity is

$$
P(dx)=p(x)\lambda(dx),
\tag{3}
$$

meaning that both sides give the same integral for every suitable integrand:

$$
\int h(x)P(dx)=\int h(x)p(x)\,dx.
$$

Do not read (3) as saying that $P$ assigns probability $p(x)dx$ to an actual
infinitesimal set. For a continuous distribution,

$$
P(\{x\})=0
$$

for every point $x$, even when $p(x)>0$.

## Mixed case

A distribution may contain both parts. For example,

$$
P(dx)=0.2\,\delta_0(dx)+0.8\,p_c(x)\lambda(dx).
$$

Then

$$
\int h(x)P(dx)=0.2h(0)+0.8\int h(x)p_c(x)\,dx.
$$

This is one reason measure notation is more general than writing only a PMF or
only a Lebesgue density.

# Conditional probability measures and kernels {#notation-probability-kernels}

Bayesian hierarchies often contain notation such as

$$
P(dx\mid\theta),
\qquad
\pi(d\theta\mid x),
\qquad
\Pi(df\mid x_{1:n}).
$$

The vertical bar changes **which probability measure is being used**. It does
not change $dx$, $d\theta$, or $df$ into a quotient.

For example, suppose $\theta$ is a parameter and $P_\theta$ is the sampling
distribution at that parameter value. Then

$$
P(dx\mid\theta)=P_\theta(dx)
$$

means “integrate over possible data values $x$ using the sampling distribution
selected by the fixed value $\theta$.” If the model is dominated by $\nu$,
then

$$
P(dx\mid\theta)=p(x\mid\theta)\nu(dx).
$$

Here $p(x\mid\theta)$ is a density in $x$ for each fixed $\theta$.

## A probability kernel {#notation-kernel-definition}

The family $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ can be represented by

$$
K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A).
$$

It is called a **probability kernel** (or Markov kernel) when

1. for each fixed $\theta$, the map $A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability
   measure on data space;
2. for each fixed measurable event $A$, the map
   $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is measurable.

The second condition makes it legitimate to average $P_\theta(A)$ over a
prior for $\theta$. This use of “kernel” is broader than a **density kernel**
such as a normal density in a mixture model: a probability kernel is a family
of whole probability measures and need not possess densities.

## Prior, joint law, and marginal law {#notation-joint-marginal}

Suppose

$$
\theta\sim\pi,
\qquad
X\mid\theta\sim P_\theta.
$$

The prior $\pi$ and sampling kernel determine the joint probability law. For
measurable sets $B$ in parameter space and $A$ in data space,

$$
P(\theta\in B,X\in A)
=\int_B P_\theta(A)\pi(d\theta).
$$

The shorthand $P_\theta(dx)\pi(d\theta)$ refers to this joint construction;
it is not ordinary multiplication of two numbers. Integrating out $\theta$
gives the prior predictive, or marginal, distribution

$$
m(A)=\int_\Theta P_\theta(A)\pi(d\theta).
$$

In a dominated model its density is

$$
m(x)=\int_\Theta p(x\mid\theta)\pi(d\theta).
$$

For a fixed observed $x$ with $0<m(x)<\infty$, Bayes' rule gives the posterior
measure

$$
\pi(d\theta\mid x)
=\frac{p(x\mid\theta)\pi(d\theta)}
{\int_\Theta p(x\mid\vartheta)\pi(d\vartheta)}.
$$

This is the ordinary parametric template for Walker's formula. Replace the
parameter $\theta$ by an entire density $f$, replace $\pi$ by $\Pi$, and use
$P_f$ as the sampling kernel.

## Conditioning on an exact continuous value {#notation-regular-conditionals}

When $X$ is continuous, $P(X=x)=0$, so this formula is **not** obtained by
dividing
$P(\theta\in B,X=x)$ by $P(X=x)$. Instead, it is a version of a
**regular conditional distribution**: a measurable family of probability
measures indexed by the possible observed value $x$.

The existence of such conditional laws is a technical theorem for the
well-behaved spaces normally used in statistics, including countable spaces
and Euclidean spaces. Two versions may differ at $x$ values belonging to a
set of marginal probability zero, just as two densities may differ on a
Lebesgue-null set. The density formula above selects the standard version
used for Bayesian inference wherever $m(x)>0$; values on the remaining
marginal-null set can be defined arbitrarily to complete a version.

Exactly the same reading applies to Walker's notation. For each fixed dataset
$x_{1:n}$,

$$
A\longmapsto\Pi(A\mid x_{1:n})
$$

is a probability measure on the model space. In $\Pi(df\mid x_{1:n})$, the
symbol $df$ still indicates that the generic model-space point is an entire
density $f$; the conditioning bar selects the posterior measure appropriate
to the observed dataset.

Authors often use uppercase $X_{1:n}$ when the data are still random and
lowercase $x_{1:n}$ for their realized values. Thus
$\Pi(\,\cdot\mid X_{1:n})$ is a random posterior measure before the sample is
known, while $\Pi(\,\cdot\mid x_{1:n})$ is the fixed posterior measure obtained
after the observed values are inserted.

The reusable parametric-to-nonparametric translation is:

| Role | Ordinary parametric Bayes | Walker's density-space Bayes |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown object | $\theta$ | Entire density $f$ |
| Prior measure | $\pi(d\theta)$ | $\Pi(df)$ |
| Conditional sampling law | $P_\theta(dx)=P(dx\mid\theta)$ | $P_f(dx)=P(dx\mid f)$ |
| Dominated iid likelihood | $\prod_i p(X_i\mid\theta)$ | $\prod_i f(X_i)$ |
| Posterior measure | $\pi(d\theta\mid X_{1:n})$ | $\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n})$ |
| Predictive probability of $A$ | $\int P_\theta(A)\pi(d\theta\mid X_{1:n})$ | $\int P_f(A)\Pi(df\mid X_{1:n})$ |

# A warning about likelihood notation {#notation-likelihood}

For a continuous model, $P_f(X=x)=0$. The contribution $f(x)$ to a likelihood
is a **density value relative to a chosen dominating measure**, not the
probability of observing the exact point.

Suppose every sampling distribution $P_f$ is dominated by the same measure
$\lambda$ and

$$
f=\frac{dP_f}{d\lambda}.
$$

For iid data, the likelihood is

$$
L_n(f)=\prod_{i=1}^n f(X_i).
$$

An expression such as $\prod_i P_f(dX_i)$ can be useful shorthand in advanced
work, but it should not be justified by calling $P_f(dX_i)$ an infinitesimal
point probability. Walker avoids this problem by working with densities
$f(X_i)$.

# Moving one level higher: a prior on densities {#notation-prior-on-densities}

Let

- $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X,\lambda)$ be the data space with a dominating
  measure;
- $\mathcal D$ be a set of candidate densities relative to $\lambda$;
- $\mathscr G$ be a sigma-field on $\mathcal D$;
- $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal D,\mathscr G)$.

Then $\Pi$ is the prior. For a measurable set $A\subseteq\mathcal D$,

$$
\Pi(A)
=P(\text{the unknown density }f\text{ belongs to }A).
$$

The notation

$$
\int_{\mathcal D}H(f)\,\Pi(df)
$$

means the expectation of a functional $H$ under that prior.

A **functional** is simply a function whose input is itself a function or
distribution. Examples are the mean $H(F)=\int xF(dx)$ and the evaluation
$H(f)=f(0)$. Here $H(f)$ produces one number from the entire candidate density
$f$.

The symbol $\Pi(df)$ should be read as

> integration with respect to the probability measure $\Pi$, whose generic
> point is the entire function $f$.

It does **not** assert that $\Pi$ has a density relative to an
infinite-dimensional “Lebesgue measure.” Such a reference measure generally
does not exist in the way it does on $\mathbb R^k$.

# Bayes' rule on the function space {#notation-bayes-function-space}

Let $x_{1:n}$ be the observed data and define

$$
L_n(f)=\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i),
\qquad
m_n(x_{1:n})=\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\,\Pi(dg).
$$

Also assume that $f\mapsto L_n(f)$ is measurable on the model space. This
ensures that the prior integrals are defined. In a density-space model this is
usually built in by choosing $\mathscr G$ so the required evaluation maps
$f\mapsto f(x_i)$ are measurable.

Assume $0<m_n(x_{1:n})<\infty$. The posterior probability of a measurable set
$A\in\mathscr G$ is

$$
\Pi_n(A)
=\Pi(A\mid x_{1:n})
=\frac{\int_A L_n(f)\,\Pi(df)}
{\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\,\Pi(dg)}.
\tag{4}
$$

Equation (4) is the rigorous statement. The shorthand

$$
\Pi_n(df)
=\frac{L_n(f)\Pi(df)}{m_n(x_{1:n})}
\tag{5}
$$

means that the posterior is absolutely continuous with respect to the prior
and has Radon-Nikodym derivative

$$
\boxed{
\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)
=\frac{L_n(f)}{m_n(x_{1:n})}
}.
\tag{6}
$$

Equation (6) is the genuine “derivative at a distribution level” in this
discussion. The normalized likelihood tells us how much Bayes' rule reweights
each region of the prior measure.

## The reason for a different letter in the denominator

In

$$
\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\Pi(dg),
$$

$g$ is a dummy integration variable. Using $g$ there makes clear that the
denominator ranges over all candidate densities, while $f$ in the numerator is
the candidate being reweighted.

# The finite case makes the notation transparent {#notation-finite-case}

Suppose

$$
\mathcal D=\{f_1,f_2,f_3\},
\qquad
\Pi(\{f_j\})=w_j.
$$

Then (4) becomes ordinary discrete Bayes:

$$
\Pi_n(\{f_j\})
=\frac{L_n(f_j)w_j}{\sum_{k=1}^3 L_n(f_k)w_k}.
$$

The notation $\Pi(df)$ is the infinite- or general-space analog of summing over
the candidates $f_j$ with weights $w_j$.

# Relation to an ordinary parametric prior {#notation-parametric-case}

Suppose $f=f_\theta$ and $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$ has a prior density
$\pi(\theta)$ relative to Lebesgue measure. Then

$$
\Pi(d\theta)=\pi(\theta)d\theta
$$

and ordinary Bayes gives

$$
\Pi_n(d\theta)
\propto L_n(\theta)\Pi(d\theta)
=L_n(\theta)\pi(\theta)d\theta.
$$

The BNP expression is structurally the same. The difference is that the
unknown point may now be an entire density, distribution, regression function,
or hazard function rather than a fixed finite-dimensional vector.

# Notation dictionary

| Notation | Safe reading |
|---|---|
| $dx$ | Integration with respect to Lebesgue measure in the present context |
| $P(dx)$ | Integration with respect to probability measure $P$ |
| $dP/d\nu$ | Radon-Nikodym derivative: a density of $P$ relative to $\nu$ |
| $P(dx\mid\theta)$ | Conditional sampling measure in $x$ selected by $\theta$; a probability kernel as $\theta$ varies |
| $\pi(d\theta\mid x)$ | Posterior measure on parameter space after observing $x$ |
| $\Pi(df)$ | Integration with respect to prior measure $\Pi$ on a space whose generic point is $f$ |
| $\Pi(df\mid X)$ | Posterior measure on that same model space after conditioning on $X$ |
| $d\Pi_n/d\Pi$ | Posterior density relative to the prior; normalized likelihood |

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. In $\Pi(df)$, is $f$ a real number, a variable in the data space, or an
entire candidate density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$f$ is an entire candidate density—a single point in the model space
$\mathcal D$. The notation $\Pi(df)$ says that integration ranges over those
candidate densities under the prior probability measure $\Pi$.
:::

**2. Why is $P(\{x\})$ not equal to $p(x)$ for a continuous model?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$p(x)$ is density height relative to Lebesgue measure, whereas $P(\{x\})$ is
the probability of a singleton. For an absolutely continuous model,

$$
P(\{x\})=\int_{\{x\}}p(t)\,dt=0
$$

even when $p(x)>0$.
:::

**3. What assumption is required before $dP/d\nu$ exists?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The essential condition is absolute continuity: $P\ll\nu$, meaning every
$\nu$-null set is also $P$-null. Under the usual Radon--Nikodym conditions
(satisfied here when $P$ is a probability measure and $\nu$ is sigma-finite),
this guarantees a density $dP/d\nu$, unique $\nu$-almost everywhere.
:::

**4. Rewrite (5) as a formula for $\Pi_n(A)$.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For every measurable $A\subseteq\mathcal D$,

$$
\Pi_n(A)
=\int_A\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)\Pi(df)
=\frac{\int_A L_n(f)\Pi(df)}
{\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\Pi(dg)}.
$$

This setwise statement is what the shorthand posterior formula means.
:::

**5. Which expression in this note is genuinely a derivative of one measure
with respect to another?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

In the Bayesian update, it is the Radon--Nikodym derivative

$$
\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)=\frac{L_n(f)}{m_n(x_{1:n})}.
$$

It is the posterior measure's density relative to the prior measure. The
earlier $dP/d\nu$ is the same kind of measure-level derivative; by contrast,
$\Pi(df)$ itself is integration notation, not a derivative.
:::

**6. In $P(dx\mid\theta)$, which symbol varies during integration, and what
role does $\theta$ play?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The integration variable is the possible data value $x$. For each fixed
$\theta$, the parameter selects one probability measure $P_\theta$ on data
space:

$$
\int h(x)P(dx\mid\theta)
=\int h(x)P_\theta(dx).
$$

As $\theta$ changes, the selected sampling distribution changes.
:::

**7. What two properties make $K(\theta,A)$ a probability kernel?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

First, for each fixed $\theta$, $A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ must be a probability
measure. Second, for each fixed measurable $A$,
$\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ must be measurable. The first property supplies a
valid conditional distribution; the second allows it to be integrated over a
prior or posterior for $\theta$.
:::

**8. Write the prior predictive measure for
$\theta\sim\pi$, $X\mid\theta\sim P_\theta$.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

For every measurable data-space event $A$,

$$
m(A)=\int_\Theta P_\theta(A)\pi(d\theta).
$$

The prior predictive averages the conditional sampling probabilities under
the prior. If every $P_\theta$ has density $p(x\mid\theta)$ relative to the
same $\nu$, then $m(x)=\int p(x\mid\theta)\pi(d\theta)$ is its density.
:::

**9. Why can $\pi(d\theta\mid x)$ be meaningful when a continuous model has
$P(X=x)=0$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

It is a regular conditional distribution, not the elementary ratio
$P(\theta\in B,X=x)/P(X=x)$. In a dominated model, Bayes' density formula
defines a version of the conditional probability measure:

$$
\pi(d\theta\mid x)
=\frac{p(x\mid\theta)\pi(d\theta)}{m(x)}.
$$

Regular conditional distributions are determined only up to sets of marginal
probability zero, just as densities are determined only up to null sets.
:::
